context: a letter from J. D. Hooker, which you are answering
exchanges:
What do you think of Ramsays Lake glacial theory?— I think the enclosed may interest you as it does me.— if not pray take the will & forget the deed.

I am frightfully busy & inundated with d——d visitors.— there goes the bell— just as I wrote!

Ever yours affec | J D Hooker

I am specially obliged to you for sending me Haasts communications. They are very interesting, & grand about Glacial & drift or marine glacial.— I see he alludes to whole southern hemisphere. I wonder whether he has read the Origin.— Considering your facts on the Alpine plants of N. Zealand & remarks, I am particularly glad to hear of the geological evidence of glacial action. I presume he is sure to collect & send over the mountain “Rat” of which he speaks; I long to know what it is. A Frog & Rat together would to my mind prove former connection of N. Zealand to some continent; for I can hardly suppose that the Polynesians introduced the Rat as game, though so esteemed in the Friendly Islands.

Ramsay sent me his paper & asked my opinion on it. I agree with you & think highly of it. I cannot doubt that it is to large extent true: my only doubt is that in a much disturbed country, I shd. have thought that some depressions, & consequently lakes, would have almost certainly have been left— I suggested a careful consideration of mountainous Tropical countries, such as Brazil, peninsula of India &c; if lakes are there very rare, I shd. fully subscribe to Ramsay’s views. What presumption, as it seems to me, in the Council of Geolog. Socy.: that it hesitated to publish the paper.—

We return home on the 30th.— I have made up my mind, if I can keep up my courage, to start on the Saturday for Cambridge & stay the last few days of the Assoc.ⁿ there. I do so hope that you may be there then.—

Farewell | C. Darwin
